{{Short description|Term in geophysics}}
The '''barotropic vorticity equation''' assumes the atmosphere is nearly [[barotropic]], which means that the direction and speed of the [[geostrophic wind]] are independent of height.  In other words, there is no vertical [[wind shear]] of the geostrophic wind.  It also implies that thickness contours (a proxy for temperature) are parallel to upper level height contours.  In this type of atmosphere, high and low pressure areas are centers of warm and cold temperature anomalies.  Warm-core highs (such as the [[subtropical ridge]] and the Bermuda-Azores high) and [[cold-core low]]s have strengthening winds with height, with the reverse true for cold-core highs (shallow Arctic highs) and warm-core lows (such as [[tropical cyclone]]s).<ref>{{cite book|title=Atmospheric Science: An Introductory Survey|author=Wallace, John M. and Peter V. Hobbs|year=1977|isbn=0-12-732950-1|publisher=Academic Press, Inc.|pages=384–385}}</ref>

A simplified form of the [[vorticity equation]] for an inviscid, [[divergence]]-free flow ([[Solenoidal vector field|solenoidal]] velocity field), the '''barotropic vorticity equation''' can simply be stated as<ref>{{cite book 
  | title = An Introduction to Global Spectral Modeling
  | author1 = T. N. Krishnamurti
  | author2 = H. S. Bedi
  | author3 = V. M. Hardiker
  | author4 = L. Ramaswamy
  | edition = 2
  | publisher = Birkhäuser
  | year = 2006
  | isbn = 978-0-387-30254-6
  }}</ref>

:<math>\frac{D \eta}{D t} = 0,</math>

where {{sfrac|''D''|''Dt''}} is the [[material derivative]] and

:<math>\eta = \zeta + f</math>

is ''absolute [[vorticity]]'', with ''ζ'' being ''relative vorticity'', defined as the vertical component of the [[curl (mathematics)|curl]] of the fluid velocity and ''f'' is the ''[[Coriolis parameter]]''

:<math>f = 2 \Omega \sin \varphi,</math>

where Ω is the [[angular frequency]] of the planet's rotation (Ω = {{val|0.7272|e=-4|u=s<sup>−1</sup>}} for the earth) and ''φ'' is [[latitude]].

In terms of ''relative vorticity'', the equation can be rewritten as

:<math>\frac{D \zeta}{D t} = -v \beta,</math>

where ''β''&nbsp;=&nbsp;{{sfrac|∂''f''|∂''y''}} is the variation of the ''Coriolis parameter'' with distance ''y'' in the north–south direction and ''v'' is the component of velocity in this direction.

In 1950, Charney, Fjørtoft, and [[John von Neumann|von Neumann]] integrated this equation (with an added [[diffusion]] term on the [[Left-hand side and right-hand side of an equation|right-hand side]]) on a [[computer]] for the first time, using an observed field of 500&nbsp;[[pascal (unit)|hPa]] [[geopotential height]] for the first timestep.<ref>
{{Citation 
 | last1 = Charney | first1 = J. G. | last2 = Fjørtoft | first2 = R.
 | last3 = von Neumann | first3 = J.
 | title = Numerical Integration of the Barotropic Vorticity Equation
 | journal = Tellus | volume = 2 | year = 1950 | issue = 4 | pages = 237–254
 | doi=10.3402/tellusa.v2i4.8607
| bibcode = 1950TellA...2..237C | doi-access = free }}</ref>  This was one of the first successful instances of [[numerical weather prediction]].
